newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian rural sector welcomes thrust of budget.
newsitem.headline: Australian rural sector welcomes thrust of budget.

text.p: Australia's rural sector welcomed some aspects of the Australian Federal budget for 1997/98 unveiled on Tuesday but had reservations about lack of detail.

An additional allocation of A$76 million over the next four years for the Australian Quarantine and Inspection Service (AQIS) was universally praised as beneficial for rural exports and for protection of the sector in Australia.

But farm organisations questioned whether the four-year A$200 million rural policy package, to replace what Treasurer Peter Costello described as an "ineffective" Rural Adjustment Scheme, would produce net benefits for the rural sector.
The Rural Adjustment Scheme offered subsidised interest rates to farmers. The rural policy package, however, is so far devoid of detail, farm groups said.
"Some specific initiatives hold promise. We welcome the substantial boost in funding for quarantine," Wendy Craik, executive director of the National Farmers' Federation (NFF) said.
A A$44 million allocation for reform of the meat inspection service, with quality control to be put in place by industry, was also welcome, she said.
But on the A$200 million allocation for the new rural policy package, Craik said "we will be interested to see details".
She said the NFF was concerned about the winding down of rural interest rate subsidies under the Rural Adjustment Scheme.
"We will want to see what transitional measures are before the new package comes into place," she said.
Craik also said the NFF was pleased to see the A$1.25 billion coming out of the National Heritage Trust for an environmental restoration programme.
"But we really are appalled that credits and rebates, an election commitment, for land care have not been delivered," she said.
"(Overall for the rural sector) there are certainly some wins but obviously we'll want to see details of the rural policy package because it's going to be a big part of the overall system," she said.
On Costello's criticism of the Rural Adjustment Scheme, Craik said there was no real evidence to show that interest rate subsidies for farmers did not achieve their purpose.
"It's important what is put in its place and that people aren't left hanging out to dry," she said.
Ian Donges, president of the New South Wales Farmers Association, welcomed the A$1.6 billion underlying surplus announced by the Treasurer, together with low underlying inflation and growth rates.

"At the end of the day that spells good news for farmers," he said. Low inflation should translate into low interest rates and hopefully keep the costs of farming down, an essential requirement in a world competitive environment, he said.
However, Donges described the rural policy package as an apparent "re-badging" of the Rural Adjustment Scheme.
"We're not too sure whether that amount of money will be beneficial to farming or not given that we don't know where it is going to be spent," he said.
Details would not be known until the end of the year.
The A$76 million for AQIS over four years was an effective 80 percent increase in the government contribution each year.
Not only farmers would benefit from disease prevention in Australia but overall exports would benefit from guarantees on Australian rural exports, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
